                    ### Question
                    A 70-year-old male visits his primary care physician because of progressive weight loss. He has a 20-year history of smoking 2 packs of cigarettes a day and was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus 6 years ago. After physical examination, the physician tells the patient he suspects adenocarcinoma at the head of the pancreas. Which of the following physical examination findings would support the diagnosis:?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Lymphadenopathy of the umbilicus
opb. Acanthosis nigricans
opc. Palpable gallbladder
opd. Renal artery bruits
ope. Splenomegaly

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Adenocarcinoma at the head of the pancreas can lead to bile duct obstruction, which may cause an enlarged gallbladder, making 'palpable gallbladder' a strong indicator of the disease. Lymphadenopathy, particularly umbilical (Sister Mary Joseph's nodule), can occur due to metastasis, supporting the diagnosis as well. Acanthosis nigricans is more commonly associated with insulin resistance and is not a direct indicator of pancreatic cancer, thus its relevance is unclear. Splenomegaly can occur due to splenic vein obstruction but is less common. Renal artery bruits are not typically associated with pancreatic cancer. Therefore, the most relevant findings supporting the diagnosis are 'palpable gallbladder' and 'lymphadenopathy of the umbilicus.'
